solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Revealing blouse might be tough for ladies to get into

indicators.note: the ladies' loo is put inside the word for a rough type, as if entering it

parts.note: a tough is a thuggish lout
the ladies is a women's lavatory, a WC

explanation.surface: A woman wrestles with a tight blouse that is hard to put on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tough' looks like an adjective about the blouse but is a noun, a lout.
explanation.definitionFit: A revealing blouse is one with a plunging neckline, the adjective describing such a garment.

clue.text: Sheriff's grass keeping mum

indicators.note: the turf word holds the mother word inside it, keeping it safe

parts.note: a lawn is an area of mown grass
Ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A sheriff's informant refuses to talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' (informer) and 'mum' (silent) suggest a secretive snitch; they are a lawn and a mother.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheriff is an officer of the law in the Wild West sense, a law enforcer.

clue.text: Simple creature to pursue revolutionary ancient custom

parts.note: to woo is to pursue romantically

indicators.note: turned round, so the word for ancient is read backwards

parts.note: ancient means old
use, as in usage, is custom or habit

explanation.surface: Someone sets out to chase an old revolutionary tradition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' reverses OLD to DLO.
explanation.definitionFit: This small crustacean found under logs is a lowly, primitive invertebrate.

clue.text: Out of bed around noon, for one's release

indicators.note: the waking word goes round the letter for midday

parts.note: up means risen from bed
for one introduces an example, abbreviated eg

explanation.surface: Someone up and about by midday sees that as their freedom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts N inside UP to make UNP.
explanation.definitionFit: To unpeg washing or a tent is to free it by removing its fastening pegs.

clue.text: All pieces for playing with at five o'clock must go in box

indicators.note: the compass bearing is placed inside the container word

parts.note: a chest is a large box
on a clock face read as a compass, five o'clock points roughly south-south-east

explanation.surface: At five, the toys must be packed away in their box.
explanation.walkthrough: Read a clock face as a compass, twelve north and six south: five o'clock points about south-south-east.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete set of kings, pawns and the rest, the full board-game kit, is every piece used in play.

clue.text: Athletic event's hard work: miss start also having entered

parts.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: the word for also has come in between the two verbs

parts.note: to skip is to miss out
to jump is to start in surprise
and means also

explanation.surface: An athletics contest is tough going, even with a missed beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having entered' is the insertion signal. The triple jump was formerly called this.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the old name of the triple jump, a track-and-field competition.

clue.text: Guards collecting old clubs, lifting one each?

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting means the letters are read upwards, backwards
the guards word gathers the two abbreviations inside it

parts.note: warders are prison guards
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Guards gather antique clubs, each one hoisting one up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collecting' puts OC inside WARDERS to make WARDEROCS, and 'lifting' turns it upwards. A result of 1-1 in football is the example.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawn match in which both sides score, such as a one-all football result, the question mark flagging an example.

clue.text: Edge of wheel discovered to have shrivelled up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means read from bottom to top
the two words are shrunk to a short run of letters from inside them

explanation.surface: A wheel's rim turns out to have dried and wrinkled.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside 'wheel discovered' sits ELDIS, which 'up' turns round. 'Edge' is a verb here, not the rim of a wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: To edge along is to move sideways or furtively, a synonym verb.

clue.text: Deny site could become an urban sprawl

indicators.note: the letters may turn into something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A planning objector refuses a site that might become a sprawling development.
explanation.walkthrough: TYNESIDE is the conurbation along the River Tyne around Newcastle in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: This north-east English region is a continuous built-up conurbation, an example of urban sprawl.

clue.text: Some poem confused with orator Cicero's observation

indicators.note: mixed up, so the letters of the words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A poem gets muddled with the sayings of the great Roman speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin for 'Oh the times, oh the customs!', Cicero's lament against Catiline.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin exclamation was famously uttered by Cicero in his speeches against Catiline.

clue.text: Celebrate noisily with band: I arranged backing

parts.note: a hoop is a circular band

indicators.note: going backwards, so the word for arranged is reversed

parts.note: to put something is to place or arrange it

explanation.surface: A musician parties loudly with the group after setting up the backing track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns PUT into TUP.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom means to party boisterously, making merry with lots of noise.

clue.text: Long forgotten, maybe, or needing no introduction

indicators.note: the first letter, which introduces the word, is dropped

parts.note: or is the heraldic term for gold, so golden

explanation.surface: Something long forgotten, or perhaps so famous it needs no introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' looks like a conjunction but is heraldry's word for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Olden days are long past, so things of that era may well be forgotten.

clue.text: Quite a posh residence in the East End?

indicators.note: Cockneys of London's East End famously drop the h sound

parts.note: a hall is a grand country house

explanation.surface: Is that a rather grand house in East London?
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is the traditional Cockney district of London, where an initial h goes unsounded, so 'all for 'hall'.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'all alone', meaning completely or quite.

clue.text: See a Greek MP rallying workers on estate

indicators.note: regrouping, so the letters reassemble in a new order

explanation.surface: Watch a Greek politician rousing the estate staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'workers on estate' suggests a housing estate; here it is a country estate.
explanation.definitionFit: These are people employed to look after game birds and animals on a landed estate.

clue.text: As end of chapter, closed book

parts.note: qua is Latin-derived for 'as' or 'in the capacity of'

indicators.note: only the final letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: to, of a door, means shut

explanation.surface: At the end of a chapter, the book is shut.
explanation.walkthrough: A door pulled 'to' is closed.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarto is a book size made by folding each sheet into four leaves, hence a book.

clue.text: Right to feed English dog bread that's disgusting

indicators.note: the abbreviation for right is fed the rest, taking it inside

parts.note: a pug is a small breed of dog
naan or nan is Indian flatbread

explanation.surface: Giving an English dog bread is thought revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to feed' has RT take in EPUGNAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Repugnant and disgusting are synonyms, both meaning causing strong distaste.

clue.text: Solid girl placed in sink to the left

indicators.note: in an across entry, going left means read backwards
the girl's name is put inside the word for sink

parts.note: to dip is to sink or drop
Mary is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A dependable girl gets put at the kitchen sink on the left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'placed in' puts MARY into DIP for DIMARYP; 'to the left' reverses it. 'Solid' is a noun, a geometric shape.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a pyramid is a three-dimensional figure, a solid with a polygonal base.

clue.text: Join by tying knot

parts.note: tying the knot is getting wed, so one joins a family through a wedding

explanation.definitionFit: To become part of a family or fortune through wedlock is to join it by getting hitched.

clue.text: Scrap involving Labour politicians in the past

parts.note: the left is the socialist wing, Labour being the UK party of the left
over means finished, gone by

explanation.surface: A row breaks out involving former Labour figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' suggests a fight; it is a remnant of food. Labour is Britain's main left-wing party.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrap of food remaining after a meal is a remnant, a synonym noun.

clue.text: Enough to swap tips with lover of old illustrations

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: the first and last letters of the word exchange places

parts.note: ample means enough

explanation.surface: Having enough, one swaps tips with a former partner on old pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to swap tips' exchanges the A and E at either end of AMPLE to give EMPLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Exempla are illustrative examples or anecdotes, especially moral ones in medieval sermons.

clue.text: English town's fresh flood defence

parts.note: new means fresh
Noah's ark saved him from the Flood

explanation.surface: An English town installs new protection against floods.
explanation.walkthrough: Newark-on-Trent is a market town in Nottinghamshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Newark is a Nottinghamshire market town, a specific example of an English town.

clue.text: Short skirts getting shorter? Too bad!

indicators.note: each of the pair loses its last letter, both trimmed

parts.note: a tutu is a short ballet skirt; two of them are needed for skirts

explanation.surface: Mini skirts getting ever more mini? What a shame!
explanation.walkthrough: Two TUTUs each lose their final U.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection expresses mild disapproval or regret, like 'dear me'.

clue.text: In school on Thursday: a dance and whatnot

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means placed after, so the day comes first

parts.note: taken as written
a gam is a school of whales
a jig is a lively dance

explanation.surface: At school on Thursday there's a dance and so on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school' is not a place of learning but a pod of whales, a gam.
explanation.definitionFit: A whatnot is a vague word for any object whose name escapes one, a synonym.

clue.text: To recap, not always out to be understood?

indicators.note: understood, heard spoken, so the phrase is read for its sound

parts.note: in some of the time, i.e. sometimes in

explanation.surface: Summing up, a person who is not always away needs to be understood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in some' (sometimes in, so not always out) sounds the same as the Latin-style phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: In sum means in short or to summarise, the same as recapping.

clue.text: Writer going into horrific detail about monk's end

indicators.note: the bloody word goes round the final letter

parts.note: gory describes horrific, blood-soaked detail

indicators.note: only the last letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: An author dwells on gruesome specifics about a monk's death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts K, from 'end' of monk's, inside GORY.
explanation.definitionFit: Maxim Gorky was a Russian novelist and playwright, an example of a writer.

clue.text: Who's reading this letter out loud?

indicators.note: spoken, the letter's name sounds like a word

parts.note: the twenty-first letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A puzzle asks who is reading a letter aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: The reader of the clue is addressed directly.
explanation.definitionFit: The person reading this clue is the solver, addressed as the second person.

clue.text: What one can see through stone blocks

indicators.note: the weight abbreviation obstructs the route word by sitting inside it

parts.note: via means by way of, through
ST is the abbreviation for stone, a British weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: What can be glimpsed through gaps in stone blocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blocks' looks like a noun after 'stone' but is a verb, the container signal. A stone is a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A vista is a view or prospect, especially a long one, so it is what is visible.

clue.text: Art master's responsibility, taking class for one

indicators.note: the remit word takes in a new piece in place of a letter
the new piece stands for, replaces, the numeral letter

parts.note: a remit is an area of responsibility
I is the Roman numeral one
a brand is a kind or class

explanation.surface: An art master's duty is to take a class instead of someone.
explanation.walkthrough: BRAND replaces the I in REMIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt was the great Dutch painter, an old master of art.

clue.text: Soldiers needing medic, subject to stress: most faint

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
MO is a medical officer
to test is to subject to stress or strain

explanation.surface: Troops needing a doctor under strain are about to pass out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faint' looks like a verb but is an adjective, as in a remote chance.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote, as in 'remote possibility', means slight, so the superlative is slightest.

clue.text: What you find at bottom of the author's bunk!

indicators.note: the lower end belongs to the writer's, so the owner word comes first

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself, so my
the foot is the bottom end of a bed or bunk

explanation.surface: What lies at the foot of the writer's bed!
explanation.walkthrough: 'bunk' is a bed in the surface but nonsense in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is a scornful dismissal of something as nonsense, like 'rubbish!'.
